author: atlas-editor
scope: Three locally author-checked routes with exact retained lesson targets and clearly labeled external readings. No public distribution, professional approval or observed learning is claimed.

relationTypes.evidence: A specified source or observation directly supports a bounded claim; requires an explicit claim and locator.
relationTypes.analogy: Transfer a representation or question while stating what does not transfer.
relationTypes.prerequisite: A directed required learning dependency, supported by actual target declarations; never inferred from sequence order.
relationTypes.question-shift: Sequence changes method or object; no evidential or dependency implication.

routes.title: Water and a city
routes.scope: A comparison across ideal hydraulics, an authored aqueduct, historical London and contemporary US stormwater planning. These are different cases, not the history or engineering design of one city.
routes.outcome: Separate a model output, a historical observation and a public planning choice; say which extra evidence would connect them.

steps.title: What can a flow model conserve?
steps.question: Which quantities trade off in the ideal flow?
steps.task: Read the three head terms. Describe what can change when the pipe narrows with friction absent, then explain why the separate friction setting changes the comparison.
steps.check: Identify pressure, velocity and elevation head; qualify conservation by steady, inviscid, constant-density flow in uniform gravity along a streamline.
steps.limit: The task is conceptual. The derivation needs Euler equations and directional derivatives; this route does not supply that proof or a real network design.
steps.entrySupport: Head is energy per unit weight expressed as a height. A streamline follows the direction of flow. Read the statement and scope before the derivation.

steps.title: What does an infrastructure model leave out?
steps.question: Does arriving at sufficient height establish useful capacity or a safe pipe?
steps.task: In the reading page, distinguish the endpoint-height test from pipe capacity and nominal stress. List two excluded effects that would matter to an actual structure.
steps.check: Separate height, flow capacity and stress; identify omitted losses, joints or material failure.
steps.limit: The terrain and dimensions are authored. The two translations disagree on gradient, and neither supplies a universal measured Roman gradient.
steps.entrySupport: Capacity is how much flow the stated model can carry; a height test alone does not determine it. Nominal stress is a model quantity, not a safety certificate.

steps.title: What can a case map establish?
steps.question: Does a decline after an intervention show what caused it?
steps.task: Read the statement and scope. Compare the dated attacks, the digitised map records and the deaths-per-house comparison. Explain why the handle removal cannot be credited from the curve alone.
steps.check: Keep the denominators and datasets distinct; mention the pre-removal decline and missing counterfactual.
steps.limit: Map locations are rounded, displaced plotting stacks with duplicates; ring density is not population risk. No modern health advice follows.
steps.entrySupport: A denominator states what a count is divided by. A counterfactual asks what would have happened without the intervention; it is not observed in this curve.

steps.title: Who participates in deciding what to build?
steps.question: Which questions survive after a technical option appears feasible?
steps.task: Read EPA’s planning and community-engagement sections. For an explicitly fictional stormwater proposal, list a goal, a metric and an affected group whose input is missing.
steps.check: Keep feasibility, chosen priorities and evidence of actual participation separate.
steps.limit: US green-infrastructure guidance is one institutional approach. A fictional stakeholder list does not establish participation, consent or a legal duty.
steps.entrySupport: A metric is an observable way to track a goal. Stormwater planning concerns runoff; it is not the same system as the aqueduct or the London drinking-water case.

transitions.reason: Both separate elevation, pressure and flow under stated assumptions.
transitions.limit: The aqueduct comparison adds friction and geometric assumptions; it is not a direct validation of the ideal Bernoulli picture.

transitions.reason: Move from moving water to evaluating evidence about a historical outbreak.
transitions.limit: Capacity or pressure says nothing by itself about exposure, infection or the effect of an intervention.

transitions.reason: Move from explaining a historical observation to choosing and assessing a contemporary planning process.
transitions.limit: EPA guidance is not evidence of what London officials did in 1854.

gaps: No accepted lesson here teaches participatory water governance or a situated account of residents’ experience.
No single-city archive, contemporary water-quality dataset or real engineering assessment has been selected.
Participant observations have not been performed. They are optional follow-up; public distribution has no recorded decision.
routes.transfer: A town has a convincing flow diagram and a falling illness count. Write one supported conclusion, one causal claim needing more evidence, and one decision that still needs public input.

routes.title: A woven cloth
routes.scope: Follow distinct questions about geometric structure, yarn/interlacing, agricultural measurement, a trade model and a named teaching account. No selected physical cloth or authenticated cultural pattern is supplied.
routes.outcome: Explain why a structural model cannot identify a textile’s materials, agricultural footprint, maker, exchange history or cultural meaning.

steps.title: Which transformations preserve a shape?
steps.question: Does a rectangle fit its own outline after a quarter turn?
steps.task: Use the non-square rectangle example. Identify the allowed rigid motions and explain why a quarter turn fails.
steps.check: Distinguish a half turn from a quarter turn and the outline from decoration.
steps.limit: Polygon symmetry is a comparison tool, not a classification of textile construction or cultural meanings.
steps.entrySupport: A rigid motion preserves distances. A symmetry must also place the whole chosen figure back onto itself. You do not need permutation notation for this task.

steps.title: Read the same crossing from both sides
steps.question: Which strip is visible, and how do labels change when the plan is turned over?
steps.task: Use the front/back views, trace one labeled crossing, introduce a symbolic error and repair the selected weft row. Compare the stored front relation with the visible back relation.
steps.check: Keep strip identity, mirrored column position and visible top strip separate. Explain why repairing a whole symbolic row is not evidence of physical repair skill.
steps.limit: The model has no real specimen, tension, drape or observed reproduction. The turning convention is specified for this diagram, not every textile.
steps.entrySupport: Warp labels identify the columns and weft labels the rows. Turning about a vertical axis keeps the top fixed while reversing the visible column order.

steps.title: What does a measured point describe?
steps.question: Would a soil-water observation establish the water cost of a cloth?
steps.task: Inspect the source identity, sample and instrument for one point. Explain why the synthetic storage calculation and laboratory measurements cannot supply a fibre crop’s water footprint.
steps.check: Retain the single-plot and laboratory scope; request crop, place, season, production and processing evidence before a textile footprint claim.
steps.limit: These Wisconsin observations are not cotton/flax data, a crop trial, a causal depth comparison or an irrigation recommendation.
steps.entrySupport: An observation is a recorded measurement with provenance. A separate synthetic calculation uses chosen assumptions; it does not turn that observation into crop evidence.

steps.title: Which trade claim belongs to the model?
steps.question: What does lower opportunity cost mean in the two-good model?
steps.task: Compare the two producers’ food-versus-cloth opportunity costs in the explanation. Identify the resource and constant-productivity assumptions.
steps.check: Explain a comparative-cost statement without inferring who benefits in an actual supply chain.
steps.limit: The model does not establish wages, coercion, bargaining power, environmental costs or the history of any cloth trade.
steps.entrySupport: Opportunity cost is what is given up to produce something else. Absolute output and comparative cost are different comparisons; the task uses ratios, not calculus.

steps.title: Whose account is this?
steps.question: What can one named provider’s teaching account establish?
steps.task: Use the retained Asare/Dento Mills research brief and, if accessible, its linked pages. Separate a self-description and advertised workshop from evidence of a particular object, making session or learner outcome.
steps.check: Attribute statements to the provider; leave object, maker, date, material, technique and meaning unknown where no selected object supplies them.
steps.limit: The two pages are one provider perspective. No course, loom design, image, pattern, observed practice or current workshop availability is verified here.
steps.entrySupport: The earlier source receipt locates a specific practitioner/studio account in Nsawam. It does not represent all Ghanaian kente or provide permission to reproduce patterns.

transitions.reason: Both can describe visible structure using a specified representation.
transitions.limit: Outline symmetry and over-under construction answer different questions; neither identifies cultural meaning.

transitions.reason: Move from a construction representation to asking what agricultural evidence would be needed.
transitions.limit: The selected soil data do not concern the fibres or agricultural history of a selected cloth.

transitions.reason: Move from provenance of measurements to assumptions in an exchange model.
transitions.limit: No measured soil point supplies the model’s labour costs or supports an actual trade history.

transitions.reason: Move from generic production assumptions to a named practitioner’s situated account.
transitions.limit: The model provides no evidence about this practitioner’s income, authority, motives or community.

gaps: No physical sample, maker-approved object/process record, fibre-crop evidence or actual trade chain is selected.
Participant observations have not been performed. They are optional follow-up; public distribution has no recorded decision.
routes.transfer: A geometric repeat has been matched to a photograph. Name one structural statement it may support and three claims about the cloth that still require other evidence.

routes.title: How an account becomes evidence
routes.scope: Compare document interpretation, sampling, causal questions, an explicit legal gap and one newsroom’s sourcing principles. These are different standards of warrant, not stages of a universal truth score.
routes.outcome: Attach each conclusion to a specific claim, source and method; distinguish repeated reporting from independent evidence and statistical assumptions from legal rules.

steps.title: What does a record actually establish?
steps.question: Does a conditional proposal establish a completed agreement?
steps.task: Read the selected documents and classify the proposal, acceptance and rhetoric claims. Use NARA’s linked orientation as an optional account of document analysis.
steps.check: Attach a conclusion to a passage; distinguish direct support, interpretation and missing evidence.
steps.limit: The US–Germany–Mexico pair does not isolate a single cause of US entry into war; it omits Mexican acceptance evidence and other perspectives.
steps.entrySupport: A source can establish that words were written or said without establishing that their proposal was accepted or their prediction true.

steps.title: When is a pile of accounts a sample?
steps.question: Does collecting more records make them independent and identically distributed?
steps.task: Read the definition of a random sample. Explain why ten copied reports of one account do not by themselves satisfy that model.
steps.check: Separate record count from the assumptions about how information was generated and selected.
steps.limit: An archive is not automatically an i.i.d. sample. This step supplies no population inference about the history pilot.
steps.entrySupport: Independent means one observation does not change the probabilistic information about another under the model. Identically distributed means the model uses the same distribution for each.

steps.title: Which outcome is not observed?
steps.question: Can an observed outcome supply its own counterfactual?
steps.task: Read the potential-outcome definition. For a fictional choice, name the unit, two well-defined alternatives and the one outcome that would actually be observed.
steps.check: Distinguish the causal comparison being asked for from the observations available to answer it.
steps.limit: Defining a causal effect does not identify it from historical records or prove a treatment effect. Simulated outcomes in the lesson are not real patient data.
steps.entrySupport: A unit is the person, plot or other object being compared. The two alternatives must be specified; one observed choice reveals one outcome.

steps.title: What changes when a legal rule controls a claim?
steps.question: Which fact, rule and time origin are needed before the fictional record can support a conclusion?
steps.task: Compare the receipt/delivery case, the malfunction recording and the refund-agreement case. Identify the missing transfer fact, what the recording shows and which event starts each clock.
steps.check: Separate evidence sufficiency, a stipulated legal route and arithmetic. Explain why a calendar does not establish entitlement and why an expired short-term window does not settle every other remedy.
steps.limit: The local educational exercise uses named displayed England-and-Wales provisions with differing editorial cutoffs. It certifies no common current-law snapshot or personal legal outcome.
steps.entrySupport: A legal rule names conditions; evidence supports particular facts. This exercise supplies fictional facts and withholds conclusions where a condition is missing.

steps.title: How should a report expose its sourcing?
steps.question: What should a reader be able to tell about a report’s sources and limits?
steps.task: Read the Reuters corrections and sourcing sections. Draft a fictional attribution note that identifies the source, what remains unconfirmed and how a correction would be made.
steps.check: Do not inflate one source into several; distinguish corroboration from repetition and make uncertainty explicit.
steps.limit: These are Reuters’ stated standards, not an observation that a report followed them or a universal journalism code. No real report is published by this task.
steps.entrySupport: Attribution states where information came from. Corroboration requires assessing the source relationship; repetition alone does not establish independence.

transitions.reason: Move from a particular document claim to the assumptions behind aggregating observations.
transitions.limit: Historical support does not turn the chosen archive into a random sample.

transitions.reason: Move from a distribution of observations to an intervention-defined question.
transitions.limit: Random sampling alone does not establish causal exchangeability or reveal both potential outcomes.

transitions.reason: Identify a domain where an applicable dated rule, rather than a causal model alone, controls the task.
transitions.limit: The legal step is a gap; it cannot be used as a prerequisite, accepted teaching target or legal conclusion.

transitions.reason: Move to a publisher’s stated practice for attribution and correction.
transitions.limit: A newsroom policy neither settles the legal gap nor supplies a general admissibility rule.

gaps: Participant observations have not been performed. They are optional follow-up; public distribution has no recorded decision.
The newsroom stop remains an external reading. No new journalism lesson or professional legal opinion is supplied by this route.
routes.transfer: Three news articles repeat one archive document. Write a supported document claim, a question about source dependence, and a reason neither quantity alone answers a legal or causal question.
